usage: 존댓말, neutral-polite; the default opening the moment anyone answers a call — stranger, elder, or customer-service line
Flat, non-rising intonation to a close friend whose unsaved number you just spotted on the screen; same word, same register, different tone
More formal/businesslike; leading with 네 before 여보세요 is common at work or with strangers to sound composed and attentive
Natural extension mid-call to test a silent or dropping line; the two-word combo makes the check explicit without sounding rude
examples: A: (전화 받으며) 여보세요? / B: 아, 저 준혁인데요. 지금 통화 괜찮아요?
A: (picks up) Hello? / B: Oh, it's Junhyeok. Is now a good time?
A/B exchange showing the canonical opening pair: 여보세요? triggers the caller's self-introduction
여보세요, 김민수 씨 휴대폰 맞으세요?
Hello, is this Kim Minsu's phone?
Everyday use: verifying you reached the right person right after they pick up
여보세요? 여보세요? 소리가 자꾸 끊겨요.
Hello? Hello? You keep cutting out.
Fuller situation: repeating it as a line-check when a bad connection keeps dropping — shows how 여보세요 doubles as an attention-getter mid-call
nuance: 여보세요 is the phone-only 'hello' — it derives from 여기 보세요 ('look here'), a call for attention, which is why it works as a mid-call line-check as well as an opener. Said to someone standing in front of you, it sounds like a sarcastic 'hello? anyone home?' or a joke, because in-person the greeting is 안녕하세요. The two are not swappable: 안녕하세요 asks after wellbeing; 여보세요 just opens the voice channel. Register sits at neutral-polite (the 세요 ending) — correct for strangers, elders, customer service, and bosses alike. Never clip it to 여보: between spouses 여보 means 'honey/darling', so it is bizarre and intimate to a stranger. The classic English-speaker error is using 여보세요 like 'hi' when meeting people in person; keep it strictly for phones.

structuredNuance.t: 여보세요 literally traces to '여기 보세요' — 'please look here' — a call for attention. On the phone that attention-getting function survives perfectly, which is why you can also use it mid-call as a line check ('hello? hello?'). It does NOT mean 'how are you' or 'hi'; it simply opens the audio channel.

Phone-only, neutral-polite (the -세요 ending). Correct for strangers, elders, customer service, and bosses. In person it sounds like a joke or a sarcastic snap — for face-to-face greetings the word is 안녕하세요.

안녕하세요 vs 여보세요: 안녕하세요 asks after wellbeing and is used in person; 여보세요 opens a voice channel on the phone. The two are not interchangeable. Also 네, 여보세요 (leading with 네) sounds more composed and businesslike.
여보세요 (standard) → 네, 여보세요 (formal/businesslike opener) → 여보세요, 들리세요? (mid-call line-check). Never clip to 여보 alone, which is the spousal term of address ('honey').
Using 여보세요 to greet someone in person — it is strictly phone-only; in person say 안녕하세요. Also: shortening to 여보 to sound casual sounds bizarre to a stranger because 여보 = 'honey' between spouses.

mistakes: Using 여보세요 to greet someone in person — it is phone-only; for meeting people say 안녕하세요.
Shortening it to 여보 to sound casual — 여보 alone means 'dear/honey' between a married couple, so it is bizarre to a stranger; keep the full 여보세요.
Translating 'hello, this is John' as 여보세요, 존이에요 and stopping — after 여보세요 Koreans usually add 안녕하세요 or 저 ...인데요 to introduce themselves.

english: Is now a good time to talk?
usage: 존댓말; polite check to an elder, boss, or anyone you respect — opening a call without asking first is considered slightly rude in Korean phone etiquette
반말 to a close friend or younger person — perfectly natural but only with someone you address as 반말
Would it be possible to talk now?
More formal/격식; 가능하실까요 adds extra deference — best for a first call to a stranger or an important client
Do you have a minute to talk?
Extension with 잠깐 signalling you will be brief — useful when you know the other person is busy
examples: A: 여보세요, 지금 통화 괜찮으세요? / B: 네, 잠깐은 돼요.
A: Hello, is now a good time? / B: Yes, briefly I can.
The classic A/B opener right after the other person picks up — B's 잠깐은 돼요 signals they're available but pressed
팀장님, 지금 통화 괜찮으세요? 잠깐 보고드릴 게 있어서요.
Sir, is now okay to talk? I have something brief to report.
Work use: always check before launching into business with a senior; 보고드릴 게 있어서요 gives a gentle heads-up about purpose
지금 통화 괜찮으세요? 혹시 운전 중이시면 이따 다시 걸게요.
Is now a good time? If you're driving, I'll call back later.
Fuller situation: offering a call-back shows consideration for the other person's circumstances — a mark of good phone manners
nuance: 지금 통화 괜찮으세요? is the courteous gate-check that Korean phone etiquette expects before you launch into business — launching straight in without asking is considered mildly rude, especially toward elders, clients, or a boss. 통화 means specifically 'a phone call/conversation', so this phrase is not interchangeable with the face-to-face 지금 시간 괜찮으세요? ('do you have time now?'); the word 통화 names the medium. To go casual, drop to 통화 괜찮아? with a friend; to go formal, use 통화 가능하실까요?, which sounds more deferential and businesslike. The closest alternative 지금 전화해도 돼요? ('is it okay if I call now?') works but sounds like you already called while asking — 통화 괜찮으세요? is the cleaner, more natural idiom. The English-speaker trap is calquing 'can you talk?' as 말할 수 있어요?, which asks whether the person is physically capable of speech — wrong and bizarre; the idiom is built on 통화, not 말하다.

structuredNuance.t: Literally '지금(now) 통화(phone call) 괜찮으세요?(is it okay)?' — the real function is a gate-check that says 'I respect your time, may I have it?' Korean phone etiquette treats skipping this as slightly rude, especially with superiors.

존댓말; the standard opener when YOU are the caller and want to be polite. 통화 괜찮아? is 반말 for friends. 통화 가능하실까요? is extra-deferential for first calls to strangers or important clients. Do not skip this opener when calling a boss.
지금 시간 괜찮으세요? is the face-to-face 'do you have time?' — 통화 names the phone medium, so it is NOT a synonym. 통화 괜찮으세요? vs 통화 가능하실까요?: same meaning, the latter is more deferential and businesslike.
지금 통화 괜찮으세요? → 잠깐 통화 괜찮으세요? (adding 잠깐 signals brevity) → 지금 통화 가능하실까요? (formal) → 지금 통화 괜찮아? (반말).

Calquing 'can you talk?' as 말할 수 있어요? — that asks about physical ability to speak, not availability. The phone-specific idiom is 통화 괜찮으세요?. Also, using 반말 통화 괜찮아? with a boss or client is a register error.

mistakes: Saying 말할 수 있어요? for 'can you talk?' — that asks about the ability to speak; use 통화 괜찮으세요? for 'is it a good time to talk.'
Dropping 지금 in a context that needs it — without 지금 it can sound like a general request; add 지금 to mean 'right now.'
Using flat 통화 괜찮아? with a boss or client — that is 반말; raise it to 괜찮으세요? or 가능하실까요?.

usage: 존댓말; the standard polite 'who's calling?' when an unknown number rings — honors the stranger while asking their identity
반말; only with a close friend whose unsaved number called you — sounds blunt or suspicious to anyone else
More formal/격식; 시죠 is softer than 세요 and is the standard formula at a business desk or reception
Extension; 실례지만 ('pardon me for asking') softens the direct identity question further — best for cold calls from strangers
examples: A: 여보세요? 누구세요? / B: 저 이민준이에요. 박 팀장님 계세요?
A: Hello? Who's calling? / B: This is Lee Minjun. Is Team Leader Park in?
The canonical A/B exchange: 누구세요? prompts the caller to introduce themselves and state their purpose
죄송하지만 누구세요? 잘 못 들었어요.
Sorry, who is this? I didn't catch it.
Everyday follow-up when a name came through unclearly — 죄송하지만 keeps it polite
누구세요? 어디라고 하셨죠? 성함 좀 말씀해 주시겠어요?
Who is this? Where did you say you're from? Could you give your name?
Fuller situation at an office desk: three escalating questions to pin down an unidentified caller — models the real sequence
nuance: 누구세요? politely asks a caller's identity — 누구 ('who') combined with the honorific copula 이세요, so it honors the unknown person while seeking information. It is used ONLY when you are the one receiving an unexpected or unrecognized call; if YOU made the call, the caller introduces themselves first (저 ...인데요), not the other way around. The key register contrast: 누구야? and 누구냐? are 반말 and sound suspicious or hostile ('who the heck are you?'), fine only with close friends. For business, upgrade to 누구시죠? (slightly softer) or 어디세요? — the latter literally 'where are you from?' asks for the caller's company or affiliation, not their personal name; these serve different purposes. A grammar pitfall: never add a subject particle (누구가세요 is ungrammatical — 누구 is an interrogative pronoun and stands alone). The English-speaker error is reversing the call direction and asking 누구세요? on a call you initiated, which is the caller's job.

structuredNuance.t: 누구(who) + 세요(honorific copula) — literally 'who are you (politely)?'. The real function is 'please identify yourself' for an unexpected or unknown inbound caller. It carries no hostility when said with a neutral tone.
존댓말; used ONLY when RECEIVING an unknown call. Say it with a calm tone — rising intonation sounds polite. Do NOT use 누구야?/누구냐? with anyone who isn't a close friend; those forms sound confrontational.

누구세요? vs 누구시죠?: 누구시죠? is slightly softer/more formal, standard at a business desk. vs 어디세요?: 어디세요? asks which company the caller is from, not their name — used in formal work contexts before 누구세요?. vs 누구야?: 반말, sounds hostile to a stranger.
누구세요? (standard polite) → 누구시죠? (business/formal) → 실례지만 누구세요? (extra-softened) → 어디세요? / 어디라고 하셨죠? (asking for company affiliation).
Two traps: (1) Adding a subject particle — 누구가세요 is wrong; 누구 stands alone. (2) Using 누구세요? on a call YOU made — the caller identifies themselves first; 누구세요? is for inbound unknown calls only.

mistakes: Saying 누구야?/누구냐? to a stranger — these are blunt 반말 and sound like a challenge; the honorific 누구세요? is required with anyone you don't know.
Adding a subject particle: 누구가세요/누구이세요 is wrong — it is simply 누구 + 세요.
Using 누구세요? on a call you yourself made — the caller introduces themselves first; you only ask 누구세요? when answering an unknown caller.

usage: 존댓말; asking anyone to hold the line briefly — phone, counter, or crowded space
반말; to a close friend or younger person — the full 잠깐만요 is also widely used as a less formal polite form
Could you hold for a moment?
More formal/격식; the expanded form for reception or customer service — explicitly requests patience
One moment, I'll put them right on.
Extension; holding to transfer the call — 바로 ('right away') signals minimum wait time
examples: A: 거기 예약 담당자 좀 부탁드려요. / B: 잠시만요, 바로 연결해 드릴게요.
A: Could I speak to the reservations person? / B: One moment, I'll connect you right away.
Natural A/B transfer exchange — B uses 잠시만요 as a smooth hold signal before transferring
잠시만요, 펜 좀 가져올게요.
Hold on, let me grab a pen.
Everyday use: pausing to write down what they're saying — the reason after 잠시만요 makes the hold feel considerate
잠시만요, 담당자 연결해 드리겠습니다. 끊지 말고 기다려 주세요.
One moment, I'll connect you to the right person. Please don't hang up.
Fuller situation: a call-center transfer script — 끊지 말고 기다려 주세요 ('don't hang up') is the canonical follow-up
nuance: 잠시만요 means 'just a moment' and is the all-purpose 'hold on' on the phone, at a counter, or even to slip past someone in a crowd. On a call it signals you are stepping away briefly without ending the conversation. 잠시 is slightly more formal than everyday 잠깐, but 잠시만요 and 잠깐만요 are interchangeable in practice; the 반말 form is 잠깐만 (or 잠시만), dropping the polite 요. The dividing line with 기다려 주세요 ('please wait') is register and weight: 잠시만요 is a quick, reflexive 'one sec', while 기다려 주세요 is a fuller, explicit request that implies a longer wait. For a formal phone hold, Koreans extend it: 잠시만 기다려 주시겠어요? The English-speaker error is reaching for 기다리세요 ('wait') — that is a bare command and sounds abrupt; the softening idiom is 잠시만요 plus the -아/어 주세요 request form.

structuredNuance.t: 잠시(a short while) + 만(only) + 요(polite) — literally 'just a short while, please.' In practice it functions as a smooth, automatic hold signal on the phone, meaning 'don't hang up, I'll be back in a second.'

Neutral-polite (존댓말) thanks to 요; fine for strangers, elders, and customer service. In 반말 context drop the 요: 잠깐만 or 잠시만. For formal phone holds, extend to 잠시만 기다려 주시겠어요?. Avoid the bare 잠깐만요 with a very senior person — prefer the fuller form.

잠시만요 vs 기다려 주세요: 잠시만요 is a quick, reflexive hold; 기다려 주세요 is a fuller, more explicit wait-request implying a longer pause. vs 잠깐만요: nearly identical meaning; 잠시 is slightly more formal. Neither can be replaced by 기다리세요, which sounds like a command.

잠시만요 (neutral-polite, the core form) → 잠깐만요 (equally common; 잠깐 is slightly less formal than 잠시 but both are used with 요) → 잠시만 기다려 주시겠어요? (full formal hold request; -겠어요? is appropriate for customer service) → 잠깐만 (반말, to a close friend; never to a stranger). Adding a reason after 잠시만요 — 잠시만요, 펜 가져올게요 — makes the hold feel considerate rather than abrupt.
Using 기다리세요 to mean 'hold on' — that is an order ('you, wait!'); the natural idiom is 잠시만요, and the polite request form adds 주시겠어요?. Also: 잠시 만요 (with a space) is wrong — it is one chunk, 잠시만요.

mistakes: Commanding 기다리세요 to mean 'hold on' — that is an order; soften to 잠시만요 or 잠시만 기다려 주시겠어요?.
Saying 잠깐만 to a customer or elder — it is 반말; use 잠시만요 or the fuller 잠시만 기다려 주세요.
Spelling/spacing it as 잠시 만요 — it is one chunk, 잠시만요, with 만요 attached.

usage: 존댓말; politely telling a stranger they misdialed — the honorific 거셨어요 still respects the caller while delivering the news
반말; to a friend who called you by mistake — informal and direct
I believe you have the wrong number.
More formal/격식; the hedging 것 같습니다 softens the correction — preferred at work or when speaking to an elder
여기 그런 사람 없는데요. 전화 잘못 거셨어요.
There's no one here by that name. Wrong number.
Extension; explaining first ('no such person') then labeling it a misdial — the natural Korean sequence
examples: A: 이민준 씨 계세요? / B: 아, 저희 회사에 그런 분 안 계세요. 전화 잘못 거신 것 같아요.
A: Is Lee Minjun there? / B: We don't have anyone by that name. I think you have the wrong number.
Natural A/B exchange: B explains first, then delivers the misdial conclusion with a softening hedge
죄송한데 전화 잘못 거신 것 같아요. 몇 번에 거셨어요?
Sorry, I think you have the wrong number. What number did you dial?
Everyday use: gently checking which number they meant — the follow-up question helps the caller correct themselves
여보세요? 김 과장님이요? 여기 그런 분 안 계세요. 전화 잘못 거신 것 같은데요.
Hello? Manager Kim? There's no one here by that name. I think you misdialed.
Fuller situation: a misdirected call at an office — shows the full sequence: repeat the name → deny → label the error
nuance: 전화 잘못 거셨어요 tells a caller they reached the wrong number — 잘못 is the adverb 'wrongly' and 걸다 is the verb 'to place/hang a call', conjugated as the honorific past 거셨어요 to maintain respect toward the stranger. The dialing verb in Korean is 걸다 (전화를 걸다 = 'to make a call'); do not substitute 하다 here. Softening is important: bare 전화 잘못 거셨어요 can sound curt, so Koreans cushion it with 죄송한데 ('sorry but') or hedge with ...것 같아요 ('seems like'). The 반말 form is 잘못 걸었어 to a friend. A common extra-polite form: 전화 잘못 거신 것 같습니다. The English-speaker trap is calquing 'wrong number' as 틀린 번호 — 틀리다 means 'to be incorrect/mistaken (as a fact)', so 틀린 번호 sounds like the phone number itself is defective; the Korean idiom describes the ACTION of dialing wrongly with the adverb 잘못 and the verb 걸다, not the number.

structuredNuance.t: 전화(phone) 잘못(wrongly) 거셨어요(you placed-honorific-past) — 'you wrongly placed a call.' The literal meaning IS the real meaning here: it's about the action of dialing wrong, not about the number being wrong. This is key for the 틀린 번호 trap.
존댓말; always use with a stranger caller. Bare 전화 잘못 거셨어요 can sound abrupt — cushion with 죄송한데 ('sorry but') or hedge with 것 같아요. The 반말 form for a friend who misdialed is 잘못 걸었어.
전화 잘못 거셨어요 vs 전화 잘못 거신 것 같아요: same meaning, the latter is hedged and gentler. vs 틀린 번호예요: 틀리다 describes a factual error — the number is defective — which sounds wrong; the idiom always uses 잘못 + 걸다.
The verb for dialing is 걸다 (전화를 걸다). 잘못 거셨어요 (honorific past) → 잘못 거신 것 같습니다 (formal/hedged) → 잘못 걸었어 (반말). Never use 전화 잘못 했어요 — dialing uses 걸다, not 하다.

Translating 'wrong number' as 틀린 번호예요 — 틀리다 is for factual errors, so it makes the number sound defective. The Korean idiom describes the dialing action: 잘못 + 걸다. Also: delivering it flatly to a stranger sounds annoyed — add 죄송한데 or hedge with 것 같아요.

mistakes: Saying 틀린 번호예요 for 'wrong number' — 틀리다 is for factual errors; the natural form is 전화 잘못 거셨어요 (misdialed action).
Using 전화 잘못 했어요 — dialing uses 걸다, not 하다; say 잘못 거셨어요/잘못 걸었어요.
Delivering it flatly to a stranger — add 죄송한데 or ...것 같아요 so it doesn't sound annoyed.

usage: 존댓말; telling anyone the line is bad — the intransitive 들리다 puts the fault on the audio, not on you or the other person
반말; to a close friend or younger person — same grammar, just no 요
More formal/격식; -는데요 is softer and more polished — slightly more appropriate in a business context
소리가 잘 안 들려요. 좀 크게 말씀해 주시겠어요?
I can't hear well. Could you speak up a bit?
Extension; pairing the bad-line report with an actionable request — the natural follow-up pair
examples: A: ...그래서 서류는 내일까지... / B: 여보세요? 잘 안 들려요. 다시 한 번 말씀해 주시겠어요?
A: ...so the documents by tomorrow... / B: Hello? I can't hear you. Could you say that again?
A/B mid-conversation example: B interrupts a bad line with 잘 안 들려요 and immediately asks for a repeat
죄송한데 잘 안 들려요. 다시 한 번 말씀해 주시겠어요?
Sorry, I can't hear well. Could you say that again?
Everyday use: combining an apology with the bad-line report and a repeat request — polite and complete
여기 지하라서 그런지 잘 안 들려요. 밖으로 나가서 다시 걸게요.
Maybe because I'm underground, I can't hear you. Let me step out and call back.
Fuller situation: naming the cause (underground) and offering a practical fix — models how Koreans explain dropped-signal situations
nuance: 잘 안 들려요 says the other person's voice is not coming through clearly — 들리다 is the intransitive/passive-feeling verb 'to be heard/audible', so the subject is the sound itself, not you. This is the crucial verb choice: 듣다 ('to listen') is a deliberate action the listener controls, so 못 들어요 could imply you are choosing not to listen — wrong and potentially rude. 들리다 means the audio physically isn't reaching your ear. Keep the adverb order fixed: 잘 안 들려요 ('well-not-audible') — the ungrammatical 안 잘 들려요 inverts it. For business, 잘 안 들리는데요 is softer. The nearest alternative 소리가 작아요 ('the volume is low') blames the volume specifically; 잘 안 들려요 covers any reason — static, dropout, noise. The English-speaker trap is 당신을 못 들어요, which uses 듣다 with the person as a direct object — this sounds like 'I'm refusing to listen to you'; native phrasing makes the sound or signal the subject.

structuredNuance.t: 잘(well) 안(not) 들려요(is audible) — 'it's not being heard well.' The subject is the SOUND, not you; 들리다 is intransitive/passive-feeling, so the phrase describes a technical audio problem, not your listening effort. This is why it's polite.
존댓말; usable with anyone on a bad line. For business, 잘 안 들리는데요 (-는데요 ending) sounds smoother. 반말 is simply 잘 안 들려 (drop 요). Word order is fixed: 잘 안 들려요, not 안 잘 들려요.

잘 안 들려요 vs 소리가 작아요: 잘 안 들려요 is the general bad-line report (any cause); 소리가 작아요 specifically says the volume is low. vs 못 알아들어요: that reports comprehension failure (didn't understand the words), not a signal problem.
잘 안 들려요 (standard) → 잘 안 들리는데요 (softer/formal) → 잘 안 들려 (반말). Add 소리가 잘 안 들려요 (making 소리 the explicit subject) for extra clarity.

당신을 못 들어요 — this uses 듣다 (active listening verb) with a person as object, sounding like 'I refuse to listen to you.' Always use 들리다 (안 들려요) to put the fault on the audio signal, not on your willingness to listen.

mistakes: Saying 못 들어요 with the person as object — use 들리다 (안 들려요), because the sound is what isn't getting through.
Word order 안 잘 들려요 — the adverb order is fixed as 잘 안 들려요.
Confusing it with 못 알아들어요 ('I can't understand') — that is about comprehension; for a bad line use 잘 안 들려요.

usage: 존댓말; reporting a dropped call to anyone — the subject particle 가 marks the call as the thing that dropped, not you
반말; to a close friend when redialing — the natural casual version
More formal/격식; 통화 and the observational -네요 ending sound a touch more composed — appropriate at work
The call suddenly dropped a moment ago.
Extension; explaining a prior drop when you reconnect — 갑자기 ('suddenly') emphasizes the unintentional nature
examples: A: (재연결 후) 여보세요? / B: 아, 아까 전화가 끊겼네요. 괜찮으세요?
A: (after reconnecting) Hello? / B: Oh, the call dropped earlier. Are you okay?
A/B reconnection exchange — the 네요 ending signals B is observing what just happened rather than blaming anyone
미안해요, 전화가 끊겼어요. 터널을 지나가서 그랬나 봐요.
Sorry, the call dropped. Must've been the tunnel.
Everyday use: apologizing and guessing the cause — 그랬나 봐요 ('seems that was it') is a natural way to speculate about a reason
방금 통화하다가 전화가 끊겨서 다시 걸었어요. 어디까지 얘기했죠?
The call cut out mid-conversation so I called back. Where were we?
Fuller situation: resuming after redialing — 어디까지 얘기했죠? is the natural pick-up line after a dropped call
nuance: 전화가 끊겼어요 reports an unintentional call drop — 끊기다 is the passive form of 끊다 ('to cut'), so 'the call got cut on its own.' This voice distinction is the most critical thing to get right: 전화를 끊었어요 uses the active verb 끊다 with the object particle 를 and means 'I hung up on purpose' — saying this instead of the passive can flip an accident into an accusation of deliberately hanging up, which is rude. 전화가 끊겼어요 uses the passive 끊기다 with the subject particle 가, making the call the intransitive subject. A nearby trap phrase: 전화 끊을게요 ('I'll hang up now') announces an intentional end to the call — entirely different meaning. For a more formal tone, 통화가 끊어졌네요. The English-speaker error is using the active 끊었어요 for an accidental drop — understand which voice matches the intent.

structuredNuance.t: 전화(the call) 가(subject: it) 끊겼어요(got-cut-passive) — 'the call got itself cut.' The passive form 끊기다 makes the drop seem accidental, like the call acted on its own. This is not a coincidence — it's the correct grammatical choice for an unintentional drop.

존댓말; use when redialing after any dropped call. 반말 is 전화 끊겼어. For formal contexts: 통화가 끊어졌네요 (-네요 sounds observational, not accusatory). Always include an apology (미안해요/죄송해요) when YOU are the one redialing.

전화가 끊겼어요 (passive, accidental drop, subject particle 가) vs 전화를 끊었어요 (active, intentional hang-up, object particle 를) — particle choice flips the meaning entirely. vs 전화 끊을게요: 'I'll hang up now' — a deliberate, announced end to the call.
전화가 끊겼어요 (standard) → 통화가 끊어졌네요 (formal/composed) → 전화 끊겼어 (반말) → 아까 전화가 갑자기 끊겼어요 (explaining a prior drop).

Using 전화를 끊었어요 for an accidental drop — the active voice means 'I hung up intentionally,' which sounds rude. Use the passive 전화가 끊겼어요. Also: 전화를 끊겼어요 (passive verb + object particle 를) mixes the forms and is wrong — the passive takes subject particle 가.

mistakes: Saying 전화를 끊었어요 for an accidental drop — that is the active 'I hung up'; use the passive 전화가 끊겼어요.
Mixing particles: 전화를 끊겼어요 — the passive 끊기다 takes the subject marker 가 (전화가 끊겼어요).
Confusing it with 끊을게요 ('I'll hang up') — that announces ending the call on purpose, not a dropout.

usage: 존댓말; promising to call back, neutral-polite — the -ㄹ게요 marks YOUR own intention
반말; to a close friend or younger person — drop 요 only
More formal/격식; humble 드리다 + -겠습니다 for a client, boss, or formal business context
I'll call you back in a bit.
Extension; 이따가 pins the callback to later today — more specific and more committed-sounding than 나중에
examples: A: 지금 잠깐 통화 돼요? / B: 지금 좀 바빠서요, 이따 다시 전화할게요.
A: Can you talk for a sec? / B: I'm a bit busy right now — I'll call you back later.
Classic A/B exchange: B declines with a polite reason and commits to a callback — shows the natural flow of a deferred call
회의 끝나고 다시 전화할게요. 한 시간쯤 뒤에요.
I'll call back after my meeting, in about an hour.
Everyday use: giving a rough time makes the promise feel concrete and reliable
지금 운전 중이라 다시 전화할게요. 도착하면 바로 연락드릴게요.
I'm driving, so I'll call you back. I'll reach out as soon as I arrive.
Fuller situation: explaining why AND giving a trigger (도착하면 = 'when I arrive') makes this a specific, credible commitment
nuance: 다시 전화할게요 is a personal promise that YOU will phone again — 다시 means 'again', and the -ㄹ게요 ending specifically marks the SPEAKER's own intention or commitment toward the listener; it would be grammatically wrong to use it about someone else's future action. To raise politeness toward a boss or client, swap 전화하다 for the humble 전화드리다: 다시 전화드릴게요 or the more formal 다시 전화드리겠습니다. The nearest natural alternative 다시 걸게요 uses 걸다 (the dialing verb) and is equally common; the difference in nuance is negligible. The English-speaker trap is trying to render 'call you back' with 부르다 — 부르다 means 'to call out to someone / summon them', which is physical and not telephonic; the phone verb is 전화하다 or 전화 걸다. Another trap is inserting 당신을 — Korean simply omits the second-person pronoun; the sentence stands without it.

structuredNuance.t: 다시(again) 전화(phone) 할게요(I will-commitment) — 'I will phone again.' The -ㄹ게요 ending is key: it marks the SPEAKER's own commitment and cannot be used to describe someone else's future action. It also implies the listener's preference is being considered.

존댓말; fine for any peer or neutral relationship. For seniors, bosses, and clients use the humble form: 다시 전화드릴게요 (전화드리다 = humble 'give a call'). 반말 is 다시 전화할게. The most formal business form is 다시 전화드리겠습니다.

다시 전화할게요 vs 다시 걸게요: nearly identical; 걸다 is the dialing verb, 전화하다 names the action — both are natural. vs 다시 전화드릴게요: same meaning, humble level — for seniors. vs 이따 전화할게요: the version with 이따 specifies later TODAY, making it more concrete.

다시 전화할게요 (standard polite; peer-level) → 다시 걸게요 (same meaning; 걸다 is the dialing verb, equally natural) → 다시 전화드릴게요 (humble; adds 드리다 to elevate the listener — use with bosses and clients) → 다시 전화드리겠습니다 (most formal; -겠습니다 for job interviews, first business calls) → 다시 전화할게 (반말; close friends only). Adding 이따 or a specific time (회의 끝나고, 한 시간 뒤에) makes any variant feel like a firm commitment.
Saying 다시 불러요 for 'call back' — 부르다 means to summon/call out physically, not to telephone. The phone verb is 전화하다/전화 걸다. Also: inserting 당신을 is unnatural — Korean omits the second-person pronoun.

mistakes: Saying 다시 불러요 for 'call back' — 부르다 means summon/call out; the telephone verb is 전화하다 (다시 전화할게요).
Using -ㄹ게요 for someone else's action — it marks YOUR own intention; to ask them to call, say 전화 주세요.
Adding 당신을 — 전화하다 doesn't take a person as object that way; just say 다시 전화할게요.

usage: 존댓말; voicemail prompt or asking a caller to leave word — 남기다 ('to leave behind') is the correct verb for any message or note
반말; to a close friend — direct and casual
If you leave a message, I'll pass it on.
More formal/격식; reception or a colleague relaying to an absent person — the conditional 주시면 + promise makes it sound professional
삐 소리 후에 메시지 남겨 주세요.
Please leave a message after the beep.
Extension; the standard Korean voicemail recording line — 삐 소리 is 'the beep sound'
examples: A: 이 대리님 계세요? / B: 지금 자리를 비우셨는데요. 메시지 남겨 주시겠어요?
A: Is Deputy Lee there? / B: He's stepped away right now. Would you like to leave a message?
Natural A/B desk exchange — B uses 남겨 주시겠어요? (question form) rather than an imperative, which sounds more professional
담당자가 자리를 비웠는데, 메시지 남겨 주시겠어요?
The person in charge has stepped out — would you like to leave a message?
Everyday use at an office desk — 주시겠어요? softens it into an offer rather than a command
연결이 안 되네요. 메시지 남겨 주시면 확인하고 바로 연락드릴게요.
I can't reach them. If you leave a message, I'll check it and get back to you right away.
Fuller situation: the conditional form 남겨 주시면 + a specific callback promise — models how to turn a dead-end call into a productive outcome
nuance: 메시지 남겨 주세요 asks a caller to leave word — 남기다 ('to leave something behind') plus the polite-request 주세요, softened with the implicit 좀. The verb is specifically 남기다 for leaving a message behind; do not use 두다 ('to put/place'), 놓다, or especially 떠나다 ('to depart a place'). A useful register distinction: 메모 남겨 주세요 uses 메모 ('a written memo/note') and is common at a reception desk when you will physically write it down on paper; 메시지 leans toward a voicemail recording or a relayed verbal message. The -주시겠어요? form ('would you...?') converts the instruction into a polite offer, which is preferred in business. The English-speaker trap is calquing 'leave a message' with the verb 떠나다: 메시지를 떠나세요 means 'depart from the message (place)', which is nonsensical — for leaving an object or information behind, Korean uses 남기다.

structuredNuance.t: 메시지(message) 남겨(leaving-behind) 주세요(please-do-for-me) — 'please leave a message behind for me.' 남기다 specifically describes leaving something behind for another person to find, which is exactly what a voicemail or relayed message is.

존댓말; used at reception desks, on voicemail, or by a colleague taking a message. The imperative 주세요 is fine; upgrade to 주시겠어요? for extra politeness. 반말 is 메시지 남겨. Business: 메시지 남겨 주시면 전달해 드리겠습니다 sounds professional.
메시지 남겨 주세요 vs 메모 남겨 주세요: 메모 is a written note (paper); 메시지 is a voicemail or relayed verbal message. Both use 남기다. Neither uses 두다/놓다/떠나다.
메시지 남겨 주세요 → 메시지 남겨 주시겠어요? (polite offer) → 메시지 남겨 주시면 전달해 드리겠습니다 (formal with callback promise) → 삐 소리 후에 메시지 남겨 주세요 (voicemail recording).

Calquing 'leave a message' as 메시지를 떠나세요 — 떠나다 means to depart a place, not to leave an object. Leaving something behind for someone to find uses 남기다. Also: barking 남겨 without 주세요 sounds like an order; always keep the 주세요 or 주시겠어요?.

mistakes: Using 떠나다 for 'leave a message' — 떠나다 is to depart a place; leaving a note/message takes 남기다 (메시지 남겨 주세요).
Saying 메시지를 두세요/놓으세요 — 두다/놓다 are 'put/place' objects; the idiom is 남기다.
Dropping 주세요 and barking 남겨 — without 주세요 it sounds like an order; keep 남겨 주세요 or 남겨 주시겠어요?.

english: Shall we set up a time to meet?
usage: Shall we make plans to meet?
존댓말; proposing to schedule a meeting with a colleague, client, or acquaintance — -ㄹ까요? invites the other's agreement
반말; to a close friend — drop 요 only
Let's go ahead and set a meeting.
More formal/격식; 잡으시죠 (hortative + honorific) is a gentle push — appropriate when suggesting a meeting to a client or senior
Then shall we set it for next week?
Extension; proposing a specific window after agreeing in principle — the natural next step
examples: A: 그 내용은 전화로 설명하기 어렵네요. / B: 그럼 직접 만나는 게 좋겠어요. 약속 잡을까요?
A: That's hard to explain over the phone. / B: Then meeting in person would be best. Shall we set a time?
Natural A/B transition from a call to proposing a face-to-face meeting — shows when and why 약속 잡을까요? gets used
그 건은 직접 만나서 얘기하는 게 좋겠어요. 약속 잡을까요?
That matter is better discussed in person. Shall we set a time?
Everyday use: moving from a call to an in-person meeting — the -ㄹ까요? ending invites the other person's input, not a one-sided decision
이번 주는 제가 좀 바빠서요, 다음 주 초로 약속 잡을까요? 화요일이나 수요일 어떠세요?
I'm busy this week, so shall we set it for early next week? How about Tuesday or Wednesday?
Fuller situation: proposing and offering candidate days immediately — the most cooperative form of scheduling
nuance: 약속 잡을까요? proposes pinning down a meeting — the verb 잡다 literally means 'to grab/catch' and is the standard verb for fixing an appointment or time slot; 약속을 잡다 is an unchangeable set phrase. The -ㄹ까요? ending makes it a soft collaborative proposal ('shall we?') rather than a decision or command. 약속 has a dual meaning: (a) a promise or commitment, and (b) a scheduled plan to meet — the verb 잡다 is what marks it specifically as scheduling. For more formal business, 미팅을 잡다 or 일정을 잡다 work too. The 반말 form is 약속 잡을까?; formal is 약속을 잡으시죠. The English-speaker trap is calquing 'make an appointment' as 약속을 만들까요? — 만들다 ('to make/create') is wrong here; appointments in Korean are 'grabbed/caught' with 잡다, not manufactured.

structuredNuance.t: 약속(plan/appointment) 잡을까요(shall we grab/catch it?) — 잡다 means 'to grab or catch'; in Korean, appointments are 'caught' or 'pinned down', not 'made'. This mental image helps avoid the 만들다 trap.
존댓말; soft proposal tone thanks to -ㄹ까요?. Use when moving from a phone discussion to an in-person meeting. 반말: 약속 잡을까?. Formal push to a senior: 약속을 잡으시죠 or 한번 뵙겠습니다 followed by date-setting.
약속 잡을까요? vs 미팅 잡을까요? vs 일정 잡을까요?: all use 잡다; 약속 implies a personal meet-up; 미팅 sounds more business-formal (from English 'meeting'); 일정 ('schedule/itinerary') is used for more formal planned events.
약속 잡을까요? → 약속 잡을까? (반말) → 약속을 잡으시죠 (formal push) → 그럼 날짜를 정할까요? (more explicit: shall we settle on a date?)

약속을 만들까요? — 만들다 means 'to create/manufacture'; appointments are 'caught/pinned down' with 잡다, not manufactured. Also: stating 약속 잡아요 (flat declarative) reads as a unilateral announcement rather than a proposal — the -ㄹ까요? question is what makes it collaborative.

mistakes: Saying 약속을 만들까요? — 'making' an appointment uses 잡다, not 만들다; say 약속 잡을까요?.
Confusing 약속 with only 'promise' — with 잡다 it means scheduling a meet-up; the verb signals the meaning.
Using a flat statement 약속 잡아요 when proposing — the inviting form is the -ㄹ까요? question, 약속 잡을까요?.

usage: 존댓말; asking an elder, client, or boss for their availability — puts their schedule first, which is the Korean social default
반말; to a close friend — same structure, drop 요 and 으
More formal/격식; -으실까요 is extra-deferential — correct register for a first meeting request to a senior or a client
When are you free this week?
Extension; narrowing to a specific week makes it actionable and easier for the other person to answer
examples: A: 한번 뵙고 싶은데요. / B: 물론이죠. 언제 시간 괜찮으세요?
A: I'd like to meet with you. / B: Of course. When are you available?
Natural A/B scheduling exchange — B responds to a meeting request by checking A's availability first, which is the polite Korean move
한번 뵙고 싶은데, 언제 시간 괜찮으세요?
I'd love to meet — when are you free?
Everyday use: opening the scheduling conversation after expressing the wish to meet
다음 주에 점심 한번 하시죠. 언제 시간 괜찮으세요? 저는 목요일 빼고 다 돼요.
Let's grab lunch next week. When works for you? I'm open except Thursday.
Fuller situation: proposing and immediately sharing your own constraints — models cooperative scheduling etiquette
nuance: 언제 시간 괜찮으세요? asks for the other person's availability so you can schedule a meeting — 시간 괜찮다 literally 'is the time okay', functioning as 'are you free.' 언제 ('when') is an adverb here and takes no particle; 언제에 is a common but wrong addition. The -으세요 ending is neutral-polite; for extra deference toward a senior, use 괜찮으실까요?. The nearest alternative 언제 시간 되세요? swaps 괜찮다 for 되다 ('to work out') and is equally natural — the choice is stylistic. Both are more natural than 언제 시간 있으세요? (which can sound more casual). The English-speaker trap is translating 'are you free?' as 자유로워요? — 자유롭다 means 'free' as in liberty, not 'available'; availability is always expressed with 시간이 괜찮다, 되다, or 있다. Always pair this question with a concrete suggestion so the other person can respond constructively.

structuredNuance.t: 언제(when) 시간(time) 괜찮으세요?(is it okay?) — 'when is the time okay for you?' The word 시간 (time/availability) carries the meaning 'free slot', not 'free (liberty)'. Availability in Korean is always framed as a time question, not a freedom question.

존댓말; standard for anyone you don't use 반말 with. For senior or important contacts, use 괜찮으실까요? (extra deferential). 반말: 언제 시간 괜찮아?. Always follow up with your own availability so the other person doesn't have to work harder.
언제 시간 괜찮으세요? vs 언제 시간 되세요?: nearly identical meaning; 되다 ('to work out') vs 괜찮다 ('to be okay') — stylistic choice only. vs 언제 시간 있으세요?: slightly more casual. All are correct; none uses 자유롭다.
언제 시간 괜찮으세요? → 언제 시간 되세요? (equally common) → 언제 시간 괜찮으실까요? (extra deferential) → 이번 주에 언제 시간 괜찮으세요? (narrowed to a week).
자유로워요? for 'are you free?' — 자유롭다 is liberty/freedom, not availability. Use 시간이 괜찮으세요? or 시간 되세요?. Also: adding 언제에 — 언제 as a time adverb takes no particle in this slot.

mistakes: Saying 자유로워요? for 'are you free' — 자유롭다 is freedom/liberty; availability is 시간 괜찮으세요? or 시간 되세요?.
Adding a particle to 언제 (언제에) — as an adverb it stands alone here; say 언제 시간 괜찮으세요?.
Using 반말 언제 시간 괜찮아? with a boss or client — raise it to 괜찮으세요? or 괜찮으실까요?.

english: I think I'll be a little late.
usage: I think I'll be a bit late.
존댓말; hedged warning to anyone you're meeting — the -ㄹ 것 같아요 frame softens bad news into an apologetic prediction
반말; to a close friend — same hedge, drop 요
I'm afraid I'll be slightly late.
More formal/격식; -습니다 for work meetings or a senior — 조금 (Sino-Korean nuance) sounds slightly more formal than 좀
차가 막혀서 10분 정도 늦을 것 같아요.
Traffic's bad, so I'll be about 10 minutes late.
Extension; giving the reason (traffic) and the approximate delay — the complete heads-up message you send when running late
examples: A: 지금 어디예요? / B: 미안, 지하철이 좀 밀려서 10분 정도 늦을 것 같아.
A: Where are you now? / B: Sorry, the subway is packed so I think I'll be about 10 minutes late.
Natural A/B lateness notification — B gives reason + specific estimate, which is the considerate Korean way
죄송한데 좀 늦을 것 같아요. 5분만 기다려 주시겠어요?
Sorry, I'll be a little late. Could you wait five minutes?
Everyday use: combining an apology, a hedged prediction, and a specific wait request — the polished three-part formula
팀장님, 지하철이 연착돼서 조금 늦을 것 같습니다. 먼저 시작하고 계세요.
Sir, the subway is delayed so I'll be a bit late. Please start without me.
Fuller situation: notifying a boss, using -습니다 for formality, and the considerate 먼저 시작하고 계세요 ('please start without me')
nuance: 좀 늦을 것 같아요 hedges a lateness warning with the -ㄹ 것 같다 ('it seems I will') frame — this is precisely the softening Korean expects when delivering inconvenient news like tardiness; bare 늦어요 sounds like a blunt, unapologetic fact. 좀 ('a bit') further cushions the degree. The verb is 늦다 ('to be late as a person'); for a transit vehicle use 연착되다/지연되다. The degree scale: 좀 늦을 것 같아요 (mild hedge) → 조금 늦겠어요 (more assertive/formal prediction) → 많이 늦을 것 같아요 (significantly late). The dividing line between 늦을 것 같아요 and 늦겠어요 is hedged-apologetic vs more confident/abrupt; -ㄹ 것 같아요 suits the apologetic social context better. The English-speaker trap is the flat 늦어요 ('I'm late') — that announces a present fact without any apology or mitigation; native speakers always wrap the lateness prediction in 죄송한데/미안한데 ... -ㄹ 것 같아요.

structuredNuance.t: 좀(a bit) 늦을(late-future) 것 같아요(it seems) — 'it seems I'll be a bit late.' The -ㄹ 것 같다 frame is not mere uncertainty — it's the polite Korean way to deliver bad news as a softened prediction rather than an abrupt statement. The hedge IS the apology.

존댓말; the standard way to warn anyone you're running late. ALWAYS lead with 죄송한데/미안한데 before it. 반말: 좀 늦을 것 같아. Formal (to boss): 조금 늦을 것 같습니다. Never deliver the bare 늦어요 as a lateness warning — it sounds unapologetic.

좀 늦을 것 같아요 vs 늦겠어요: -ㄹ 것 같아요 is hedged and apologetic; -겠어요 is a more assertive (and slightly abrupt) prediction. vs 늦어요: that's a present-tense fact ('I'm late now'), not a heads-up warning. vs 못 갈 것 같아요: 'I might not make it' — stronger and often triggers a reschedule.
좀 늦을 것 같아요 → 10분 정도 늦을 것 같아요 (give the specific delay) → 차가 막혀서 좀 늦을 것 같아요 (add reason) → 조금 늦을 것 같습니다 (formal).
Flat 늦어요 as a warning — that's a blunt present-tense statement with no apology; wrap it in 죄송한데/미안한데 + 늦을 것 같아요. Also: 늦었어요 (past) is 'I was/am already late' — don't use it as a future warning.

mistakes: Saying flat 늦어요 to warn of lateness — it sounds blunt; hedge with 좀 늦을 것 같아요 and add 죄송한데.
Using 늦었어요 (past) when you haven't arrived yet — that means 'I was/am already late'; for a prediction use 늦을 것 같아요.
Confusing 늦다 with 느리다 — 느리다 is 'slow (speed)'; being late to an appointment is 늦다.

english: Could we push the appointment back?
usage: 존댓말; the polite permission frame -아도 될까요? asks for the other person's consent rather than announcing unilaterally
반말; to a close friend — 좀 softens slightly even in 반말
Would it be alright to postpone?
More formal/격식; 괜찮으실까요 is extra-deferential — appropriate for a client or senior you are inconveniencing
혹시 약속을 다음 주로 미뤄도 될까요?
Could we possibly move it to next week?
Extension; proposing the new timing alongside the request — the considerate way to reschedule
examples: A: 내일 약속 말이에요. / B: 죄송한데 약속을 미뤄도 될까요? 급한 일이 생겨서요.
A: About tomorrow's plans. / B: Sorry, could we postpone? Something urgent came up.
Natural A/B rescheduling exchange — B leads with 죄송한데 before the permission request, and gives a brief reason without over-explaining
갑자기 일이 생겨서요, 오늘 약속을 미뤄도 될까요?
Something came up suddenly — could we postpone today's plans?
Everyday use: 갑자기 일이 생겼다 is the most common reason for rescheduling and is socially accepted without further detail
정말 죄송한데 제가 몸이 좀 안 좋아서, 약속을 다음 주로 미뤄도 될까요? 날짜는 편하신 때로 맞출게요.
I'm so sorry, I'm not feeling well — could we move it to next week? I'll fit whatever date suits you.
Fuller situation: full apology + reason + proposed new timing + offer of flexibility — the gold standard for a reschedule request
nuance: 약속을 미뤄도 될까요? asks permission to postpone a plan — 미루다 ('to put off / push back') plus the permission frame -아도 될까요? ('would it be okay if...?'). The -아도 될까요? structure explicitly makes it a request for the other's consent, not a unilateral decision — this is the socially correct frame when YOU are the one inconveniencing them. 미루다 means push to a later time within the same general intent to meet; cancelling outright is 취소하다. This distinction matters: saying 약속을 취소해도 될까요? when you mean to reschedule can alarm the other person because 취소 means the plan is off entirely. The formal versions: 미뤄도 괜찮으실까요? (extra deferential). The English-speaker trap is the assertive 약속을 미뤄요 or the bare 약속을 미룰게요 — these sound like unilateral announcements; the permission question is what makes it polite.

structuredNuance.t: 약속을(the appointment) 미뤄도(even if postponed) 될까요?(would it be okay?) — 'would it be okay if I postponed our appointment?' The -아도 될까요? frame is a genuine request for the other person's permission, not a rhetorical question — you're giving them the power to say no.
존댓말; ALWAYS precede with 죄송한데/죄송하지만 when calling to reschedule — Korean social norms expect you to acknowledge the inconvenience explicitly. 반말: 약속 좀 미뤄도 돼?. Formal: 약속을 좀 미뤄도 괜찮으실까요?.

약속을 미루다 vs 약속을 취소하다: 미루다 = postpone (intent to meet stays intact); 취소하다 = cancel (meeting is off). Using 취소 when you mean 미루다 can worry or offend. vs 약속을 바꾸다: 'change the appointment' — also acceptable but less common for time-shifting.
약속을 미뤄도 될까요? → 약속을 미뤄도 괜찮으실까요? (extra deferential) → 약속을 다음 주로 미뤄도 될까요? (with proposed new time) → 약속 좀 미뤄도 돼? (반말).

Announcing 약속을 미룰게요 ('I'll postpone our appointment') — that's a unilateral statement, not a request for permission, which sounds presumptuous. Use the question form -아도 될까요?. Also: 약속을 미뤄요 is a command/statement — equally problematic.

mistakes: Saying 약속을 취소해도 될까요? when you mean to reschedule — 취소 is to cancel entirely; to push it later use 미루다.
Commanding 약속을 미뤄요 — that orders them; ask permission with 미뤄도 될까요?.
Confusing 미루다 with 늦추다 alone — both can mean delay, but for rescheduling plans 약속을 미루다 is the set collocation.

usage: 존댓말 (humble); the courteous promise to a boss, client, or elder — 드리다 lowers the speaker to honor the listener
반말; to a close friend — drops the humble 드리다 entirely
More formal/격식; -겠습니다 used in formal business contexts — standard at the end of a job interview or client meeting
I'll check and get back to you.
Extension; promising to follow up after looking into something — the -고 나서/확인하고 lead-in is the natural connector
examples: A: 그 부분은 확인이 필요해서요. / B: 네, 제가 확인하고 오늘 중으로 연락드릴게요.
A: That part needs checking. / B: Understood — I'll verify and get back to you today.
Classic A/B business follow-up exchange — B commits to a specific timeframe (오늘 중으로 = by today), which makes the promise credible
자리 나는 대로 바로 연락드릴게요.
I'll contact you as soon as a spot opens up.
Everyday use: a service promising to reach out the moment availability changes — 나는 대로 ('as soon as it comes') is the natural trigger
지원해 주셔서 감사합니다. 결과는 다음 주 중으로 연락드리겠습니다.
Thank you for applying. We'll contact you with the result sometime next week.
Fuller situation: formal post-interview close — the -겠습니다 ending and 다음 주 중으로 set a professional, specific promise
nuance: 연락드릴게요 promises future contact — 연락하다 ('to contact') in the humble form 연락드리다, where 드리다 ('to give, humbly') lowers the speaker to elevate the listener. The -ㄹ게요 ending marks YOUR own intention. 연락 is medium-neutral: it covers a phone call, text, email, or any channel, making it broader and more flexible than 전화할게요 (phone only). The dividing line is channel-specific (전화 = phone call) vs open-channel (연락 = any contact method). To go plain-polite (peers): 연락할게요; to go casual (friends): 연락할게; to go formal: 연락드리겠습니다. The English-speaker trap is inserting 당신에게 — 당신 to a real second person sounds confrontational or awkwardly intimate in Korean; simply omit it. Another grammar trap is 연락이 될게요, which incorrectly mixes the passive 되다 with the intentional -ㄹ게요.

structuredNuance.t: 연락(contact) 드릴게요(I will give humbly-commitment) — the 드리다 ('give humbly') is the humble form, meaning you are 'giving the act of contacting' to the listener as a service. This is a structural humility marker, not just politeness vocabulary.
The humble 연락드릴게요 is for bosses, clients, and elders. With a peer use 연락할게요; with a close friend 반말 is 연락할게. The formal version is 연락드리겠습니다 (-겠습니다 for job-interview / business letter level).
연락드릴게요 vs 전화드릴게요: 연락 is medium-neutral (any channel); 전화 is phone-only. If you are not sure how you'll contact them, 연락드릴게요 is safer. vs 이따 연락드릴게요: adds 이따 (later today) to make it more concrete.
연락드릴게요 → 연락드리겠습니다 (formal) → 연락할게요 (plain polite) → 연락할게 (반말) → 확인하고 연락드릴게요 (with follow-up trigger).

Inserting 당신에게 — 당신 to a real addressee sounds confrontational or oddly intimate; Korean simply omits the second-person pronoun. Also: 연락이 될게요 is wrong — the speaker's promise uses active 연락드리다 + -ㄹ게요, not 되다.

mistakes: Inserting 당신에게 — 당신 sounds confrontational/odd to a real listener; just say 연락드릴게요 and omit the pronoun.
Using plain 연락할게요 to a client or boss — prefer the humble 연락드릴게요 to show respect.
Saying 연락이 될게요 — the speaker's intention uses active 연락하다/연락드리다 + -ㄹ게요, not 되다.

usage: 존댓말 (humble); promising to phone a boss, client, or elder later the same day — 드리다 elevates the listener
반말; to a close friend — drop the humble 드리다 and use plain 하다
More formal/격식; -겠습니다 in a business context — sounds measured and professional
Extension; 저녁에 narrows the later-today window to the evening — turns a vague promise into a concrete commitment
examples: A: 지금 잠깐 얘기할 수 있어요? / B: 지금 회의 중이라서요. 이따 전화드릴게요.
A: Can we talk briefly now? / B: I'm in a meeting. I'll call you later.
Classic A/B polite deferral — B gives a brief reason and the specific this-day promise makes it more than a brush-off
회의 중이라서요, 이따 전화드릴게요. 한 시쯤 괜찮으세요?
I'm in a meeting, so I'll call you later. Is around one okay?
Everyday use: giving a rough time (한 시쯤 = around 1 o'clock) alongside the promise makes it concrete and considerate
지금 손님이 계셔서 통화가 어려워요. 이따 일 끝나고 전화드릴게요.
I have a customer right now so I can't talk. I'll call you after work.
Fuller situation: stating the obstacle and the trigger event (일 끝나고 = after work) — the complete, credible callback formula
nuance: 이따 전화드릴게요 promises to call later today — 이따(가) is the adverb 'in a while / later (same day)', so it is near-term and specific to today, unlike 나중에 ('sometime later', open-ended). This distinction is socially meaningful: 이따 전화드릴게요 feels like a genuine commitment; 나중에 전화할게요 can read as a brush-off, especially if said to a person who needs a prompt answer. 전화드리다 (humble form) + -ㄹ게요 (speaker's intention) make this the correct formula for addressing seniors. The 반말 is 이따 전화할게. For business, 이따 전화드리겠습니다. Spelling trap: 이따 is the 'later' adverb — do NOT write 있다가, which is the verb 있다 + -다가 ('after being/staying somewhere'), a completely different grammar structure. The English-speaker trap is reaching for 나중에 when 이따 is the right precision.

structuredNuance.t: 이따(later today) 전화(call) 드릴게요(I will give humbly-commitment) — 이따 is key: it pins the callback to the same day, making this a concrete near-term promise, not a vague 'someday.' This is the word that separates a genuine commitment from a polite brush-off.

존댓말 (humble); for bosses, clients, elders. 반말: 이따 전화할게. Formal: 이따 전화드리겠습니다. Add a time if possible (이따 두 시쯤 = around 2) to make the promise more credible. Do NOT use 이따 for something that might be tomorrow — 내일 전화드릴게요 is more honest.

이따 vs 나중에: 이따 = later today (specific, committed); 나중에 = sometime later (vague, can sound like a brush-off). vs 곧 전화드릴게요 ('I'll call soon'): even more immediate than 이따 — implies minutes rather than hours.
이따 전화드릴게요 → 이따 저녁에 전화드릴게요 (with time of day) → 이따 전화드리겠습니다 (formal) → 이따 전화할게 (반말) → 이따 두 시쯤 전화드릴게요 (with specific time).

Writing 있다가 for 이따 — 있다가 is 있다 + -다가 ('after being/staying somewhere'), a different grammar word entirely. The 'later today' time adverb is 이따(가). Also: using 나중에 when you mean later today weakens the commitment and can sound like avoidance.

mistakes: Writing 있다가 for 'later' — that is the verb 있다 + -다가 ('after being'); the time adverb is 이따(가).
Saying 나중에 전화할게요 when you mean later the same day — 나중에 is open-ended and can sound like a brush-off; use 이따.
Using plain 전화할게요 to an elder or boss — prefer the humble 전화드릴게요.

english: Could you give me your number?
usage: Please give me your phone number.
존댓말; the standard polite request — 좀 softens it from a demand into 'if you would'
반말; to a close friend or younger person — equally natural in a casual context
Could you give me your contact info?
More formal/격식; 연락처 covers phone number and/or email; -주시겠어요? makes it an offer question, appropriate in business
혹시 전화번호 좀 알 수 있을까요?
Could I possibly get your number?
Extension; extra-tentative phrasing with 혹시 ('perhaps') + 알 수 있을까요? — ideal when asking a stranger or someone senior you don't know well
examples: A: 다음에 연락드릴게요. / B: 네, 전화번호 좀 알려 주시겠어요?
A: I'll get in touch next time. / B: Sure, could you give me your number?
Natural A/B exchange at the end of a call or meeting — B transitions the conversation into a number exchange
나중에 연락드릴게요. 전화번호 좀 알려 주세요.
I'll get in touch later — could you give me your number?
Everyday use: asking so you can follow up — the sequential phrasing (연락드릴게요 → 번호 주세요) models natural Korean flow
예약 확인 문자를 보내 드릴게요. 연락처 좀 알려 주시겠어요?
I'll text you a booking confirmation. Could you give me your contact number?
Fuller situation: a staffer taking a number for a reservation — the reason given first (문자를 보내 드릴게요) makes the request feel purposeful and trustworthy
nuance: 전화번호 좀 알려 주세요 politely asks for a phone number — 알리다 ('to let someone know / inform') plus the request 주세요, with 좀 ('just a little') softening the whole thing into a gentle ask. The verb must be 알려 주다: do NOT use 가르치다 ('to teach'), which is for teaching a skill or subject; 번호를 가르쳐 주세요 sounds like you want a lesson in phone numbers. For business, 연락처 ('contact details', can include email or phone) is more professional than 전화번호. A very natural and honorific alternative: 전화번호가 어떻게 되세요? — this uses 어떻게 되세요?, the Korean honorific formula for asking for personal information ('how does it go?'), which is far more polite than 전화번호가 뭐예요?. The English-speaker trap is dropping 좀 and 주세요 to get the bare 전화번호 알려 — without these softeners it is abrupt and slightly pushy.

structuredNuance.t: 전화번호(phone number) 좀(just a little) 알려(let-know) 주세요(please-do-for-me) — literally 'please let me know your phone number a little bit.' The '좀' + '주세요' combination is what makes this a polite request rather than a demand; both softeners are required.
존댓말; standard for anyone. For business or seniors, upgrade to 연락처 좀 알려 주시겠어요? or the honorific 전화번호가 어떻게 되세요?. 반말: 전화번호 좀 알려 줘. Never ask 전화번호가 뭐예요? to an elder — 뭐예요 is too blunt for personal info.

전화번호 좀 알려 주세요 vs 전화번호가 어떻게 되세요?: both polite; the former is a direct request, the latter is the honorific inquiry form ('how does the number go?') — 어떻게 되세요? is the standard Korean way to ask for personal details honorifically. vs 연락처 알려 주세요: 연락처 is broader (phone + email).
전화번호 좀 알려 주세요 → 전화번호가 어떻게 되세요? (honorific inquiry) → 연락처 좀 알려 주시겠어요? (formal, business) → 혹시 전화번호 좀 알 수 있을까요? (extra-tentative) → 전화번호 좀 알려 줘 (반말).

가르쳐 주세요 for 'tell me your number' — 가르치다 is to teach a skill or subject; for sharing a piece of information use 알려 주다. Also: stripping away 좀 and 주세요 to get 전화번호 알려 sounds rude and demanding — the softeners are not optional politeness additions.

mistakes: Using 가르쳐 주세요 for a number — 가르치다 is to teach a subject; to share info say 알려 주세요.
Asking 전화번호가 뭐예요? to an elder/stranger — prefer the honorific 어떻게 되세요? or 알려 주세요.
Dropping 좀/주세요 (전화번호 알려) — it sounds abrupt; keep 좀 알려 주세요 to stay polite.
